Son Sold Dad's 1972 Pontiac Luxury LeMans After Many Years in Hiding, Restoration Now Needed
44 photos
Photo: eBay seller spoilerecw
Two owners. Oklahoma car. Original engine and transmission. Parked for years before the owner’s son decided to let it go. These are the main things you must have in mind when checking out this 1972 Pontiac Luxury LeMans.
This Pontiac landed on eBay in project car condition, so what it needs today is a restoration. This would be the first major refresh in its life, and despite the seller advertising a car that has never been “modified or tampered with,” you’ll discover that it has already received some changes.
For example, the driver’s fender has already been replaced (though the original rusty one is still available), while the grille comes from a 1971 T-37 (with two correct sets also being offered).
That is why I recommend that any restoration guy who thinks he can save this Luxury LeMans calls the seller and arranges an in-person inspection. This unrestored and unaltered promise sounds almost too good to be true, so you must see everything with your own eyes before making an offer.
Photo: eBay seller spoilerecw The Luxury LeMans wasn’t as popular as the GTO , but in 1972, it was certainly the model that brought home more bacon. Sales of the GTO were already going down after the decline started earlier in the same decade, so this model ended the year with only a little over 5,800 cars sold to American buyers.
The Luxury LeMans didn’t suffer from the exclusive performance-oriented DNA as the GTO, so it managed to convince over 46,000 buyers in 1972.
The base engine on the Luxury LeMans was a 350 rated at 160 horsepower (this was the net rating that came into effect this year). Pontiac also offered several big-block upgrades, including a 455, without giving buyers the option to order the 455-4 with a Rochester four-barrel carburetor and 250 horsepower. This engine was available on all LeMans configurations, except for the Luxury.
As for what made the Luxury LeMans luxurious, it was the focus on comfort rather than on performance. Each car was fitted with plush carpets, a padded steering wheel, and standard fender skirts. Pontiac also offered a special instrument panel, as well as a special grille, trim, and badging to make it obvious that you drove a Luxury LeMans.
This model survived in the following years, eventually evolving into the Grand LeMans when the 1975 model year came out.
Photo: eBay seller spoilerecw This 1972 Luxury LeMans has already been refreshed mechanically. It’s fitted with the base Pontiac 350 two-barrel engine paired with an automatic transmission. The carburetor was rebuilt, and the car has new brakes, new hoses, a new alternator, and so on. The gas tank has also been cleaned, but the gas gauge doesn’t work.
Otherwise, the car is in running shape, so if you want to hop in and take it for a spin, you should be able to do this during your in-person inspection.
But any diehard Pontiac guy will want to deal with the obvious problems first. There’s obvious rust on this LeMans, though I think the existing damage isn’t by any means critical. It’s just typical corrosion that a good metal guy will deal with quite easily, but that’s why I recommended that you see the car in person.
If you raise it on a lift, determining how many repairs it needs is much easier.
The windshield is also cracked, and the culprit is a tree limb that fell on the car during a storm a few years ago. Otherwise, it’s a solid restoration candidate that can also become a father-son project for the winter.
Photo: eBay seller spoilerecw Let’s be honest here. A 1972 Pontiac Luxury LeMans isn’t necessarily the most desirable car, and that’s why such a project must be priced accordingly to let it find a new home fast.
GTOs and big-block LeMans projects continue to be icing on the cake for the 1972 model year, so despite being quite a special car, a Luxury LeMans is hardly a collectible. A diehard Pontiac fanboy would obviously love to own such a car, but otherwise, it’s hard to believe that anyone would pay big bucks for such a car.
Fortunately, the seller looks realistic, so the auction they started on eBay begins at $5,000. Nobody has entered the digital fight so far, but considering a reserve is also in place, this could be why. Potential buyers might be afraid that the reserve is unrealistic, so if you want this car, you should just call the seller and ask all your questions on this front.
The auction ends in a little over 5 days, so theoretically, you have all the time in the world to arrange an in-person inspection and also go there to figure out what this car needs. The vehicle is parked in Eakly, Oklahoma, and despite its running condition, taking it home on a trailer is probably the recommended approach, considering it’s still a project.

Tesla has unveiled a new version of its next-generation Roadster. As expected, it received Tesla’s latest design “cyberfication” and cold-gas thrusters to allow it to jump and flip through the air.
The livestream featured impressive stunts but offered few details. Tesla released more information on X after the event, but there’s still no price and no production date.
Nine years in the making
Tesla first unveiled the next-gen Roadster as a prototype in November 2017 and promised production in 2020. That date came and went, and so did several more.
This year alone, Elon Musk promised an unveil in April , then late April, then “a month or so” after Q1 earnings. The demo was later pushed to August , then to October 1. Tesla finally streamed the event tonight.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The entire intro felt like Elon Musk and co. trying to create a reason to link Tesla and SpaceX ahead of an expected merger. It gave Solar Tile unveiling event ahead of Tesla’s SolarCity acquisition.
From S3XY to Cyber
Tesla confirmed that the design changed a lot since the 2017 prototype. Its design language evolved from the S3XY lineup to Cybertruck, Cybercab, and Optimus, and that the new Roadster takes inspiration from the SR-71 and the F-35.
Image: Tesla
On its updated Roadster page , Tesla describes hidden headlights, a full-length taillight, and flush-mounted aero. The “Ano White” paint is said to borrow from coatings used to protect rockets, and the tinted windows are meant to mimic the gold visor of a spacesuit.
Image: Tesla
Inside, there’s a yoke designed for steer-by-wire, a center touchscreen, and two smaller displays in front of the driver. Tesla also went with a fixed seat position and manual controls to save weight, along with magnesium, titanium, and carbon fiber throughout.
Three versions: Performance, Thrust, and Rocket
The configurations only came out after the stream, in a thread on Tesla’s X account . There are three:
Performance: road ready, seats two, active aero and a “multi-mode suction system.” 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds. Available by reservation.
Thrust: race ready, seats two, adds rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters. 0-60 mph in under 0.9 seconds. Limited release.
Rocket: seats one, adds thrusters around the perimeter of the car for upward and rotational movement. 0-60 mph in under 0.59 seconds and a top speed of over 230 mph. Invite only.
Tesla quotes a range of over 300 miles. The company’s own Roadster page states that the Rocket isn’t approved for public road use, and Tesla treats Thrust and Rocket as “augments” on top of the Performance car.
Image: Tesla
The thrusters are where SpaceX comes in. Tesla says making them work in atmosphere rather than a vacuum required new hardware and controls, and that every usable void in the car is packed with carbon-fiber overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs) to store compressed gas. More gas means more “flight time.”
Tesla claims the thrusters generate four to five times the force the tires can handle, which is how it gets around the traction limit that caps every other car’s acceleration.
The suction system does the opposite job. Tesla says its fans pull enough air from under the car to hold it upside down, even when stationary. In Track Mode , the car lowers itself and deploys active wings driven by the same actuators Tesla developed for Optimus. Tesla claims downforce “approaching F1 levels.”
Image: Tesla
What’s still missing
Tesla reopened Roadster reservations. It’s $5,000 due today, which Tesla calls fully refundable, and another $45,000 due within 10 days or the reservation gets canceled. That’s the same $50,000 Tesla asked for in 2017.
But Tesla didn’t give a price for any of the three versions, and there’s no production date other than “2028, actually”, an actual quote from Musk.
Some of the specs have also moved since 2017. Tesla originally promised 620 miles of range, a top speed above 250 mph, and seating for four in a 2+2 layout. The new car is now quoted at over 300 miles, over 230 mph on the Rocket trim, and two seats at most.
Acceleration went the other way. The base Performance trim beats the 1.9-second 0-60 mph Tesla promised in 2017, and the Thrust and Rocket claims are well beyond anything on the market, including the Rimac Nevera.
And it can also do impressive stunts:
Roadster event livestream https://t.co/G0jU4mWfid — Tesla (@Tesla) October 15, 2026
I doubt using those features will keep your warranty going, though.
Electrek’s Take
The engineering here is real. Cold-gas thrusters that work in atmosphere, a fan system that can hold a car to a ceiling, and wings run by Optimus actuators. Nothing entirely new, but I think it’s the first time that it’s all in one car, which is impressive.
But the stunts that are making the headlines are on trims that are invite-only or limited, and not road legal. They will likley null your warranty, and at the end of the day, I doubt Tesla will sell more than a handful of those for marketing reasons only.

Man Blows Almost $72K on New Fisker Ocean, Sells for Nothing 11,000 Miles Later
14 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
Fisker declared bankruptcy in 2024 due to several reasons, including a huge cash burn after launching the Ocean, but the EV is still alive and well, and it changes hands for nothing these days.
Usually, the electric crossover goes from anywhere between $14,000+ and over $30,000 in today’s used car market in the United States of America. The FWD Sport is the most affordable, followed by the Ultra, One, and Extreme in this order generally. And that’s nothing, given that it used to start at almost $38,000 for the base grade, with the Ultra, Extreme, and One kick off at nearly $50,000, over $61,000, and almost $70,000, respectively.
Pictured above is a Fisker Ocean One that is part of the 2023 model year. It features a Mariana Metallic paint finish on the outside, a Black Abyss Plus interior, and packs plenty of gizmos. The listing mentions stuff such as the SolarSky roof panel, 22-inch wheels, Hyper Range battery pack, Fisker Pulse sound system, Resolve 17.1-inch infotainment system, heated steering wheel, heated front and rear seats, and a few other things.
Power comes from a pair of electric motors that drive all four wheels. The total system output is 564 horsepower (571 ps/420 kW) and 543 pound-feet (737 Nm) of torque. This model needed just 3.6 seconds to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from zero when it was new, and its top speed was electronically capped at 127 mph (205 kph). A 113 kWh lithium-ion battery pack supplied electrons to the motors, and when it was fully charged, it enabled a 360-mile (580 km) range (EPA) with the Hyper Range battery.
Photo: Cars&Bids One may not usually expect the Fisker Ocean to have any mods, but this one does. The TPMS (tire pressure monitoring system) is said to have come from the aftermarket world. There is also a Fisker OS 2.6.1 software update, and a CarLink kit for Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The curb rash on the wheels, some chips on the front-facing surfaces, dings on the rear bumper and left rear door, and a dent on the right rear door are the only known flaws mentioned in the listing that we will link toward the end of this article.
The electric crossover in question has a clean Illinois title, and is located in Chicago, IL. At the time of cataloging, the odometer read around 10,800 miles (17,400 km), added by the first owner, who bought it new in November 2023. That’s roughly 3,600 miles (5,800 km) annually on average, so it is not exactly a high-mileage example, yet it still sold for pennies on the dollar, though that’s not a big surprise, is it?
More on the actual selling price in a few moments, as first, we also have to tell you that besides the vehicle itself, the new owner will also get the window sticker, two key fobs, two key cards, and the Vgate vLinker MC + Bluetooth OBD2 adapter. The EV is said to have had its 12-volt battery replaced earlier this year, in May 2026, though no documentation was provided, and this is the only visit it paid to the shop.
Photo: Cars&Bids The man whose name is written in the papers paid $71,687 for this Fisker Ocean One toward the end of 2023, as the attached window sticker reveals. He hasn’t revealed the motive(s) for selling the electric crossover, but he definitely took a huge loss. When the gavel hit the table, this machine ended up changing hands for $15,801. That was the selling price recorded on Cars&Bids at the end of the online auction. The event concluded just recently, on October 14, 2026, and left a big dent in the seller’s finances.
To better put that sum into perspective, this Fisker Ocean ended up costing its first owner over $5 per mile, and that depreciation simply hurts. It will be interesting to see how much this model will cost a couple of years from now, and by the looks of it, it will likely change hands on the used car market for even less money. However, the Ocean is still a lot of car for the money and a cool daily driver, though the fact that it is no longer backed by Fisker, which went bankrupt in 2024, as mentioned above, makes it sell for pennies on the dollar.
Now, the Fisker Ocean is definitely not a car for the average Joe, as only a few will dare to buy such a thing, but we have to admit that paying roughly $15K for a low-mileage and modern-day electric vehicle feels like a steal in today’s market. If you had encountered this ride in time, would you have bid on it? And if so, how much would you have been willing to pay for it? Porsche Mission S Aims to Reinterpret the Supercar for the Future: Mid-Engine, Fewer Screens, ICE
46 photos
Photo: Porsche AG
As promised and leaked before the unveiling event, the Porsche Mission S is a concept car aimed to preview the future of the supercar for the German brand. An eventual production model will not be electric, that’s for sure.
Porsche has a mission to come out of the woods of decaying profits and sales, and it’s called ‘ Sportwagenschmiede 2035 .’ Yep, Germans love these long and hard-to-pronounce words, that’s for sure! This summer we went with the family on vacation in Germany and we came back home not remembering even one place where we went to because of these difficult words…
Anyway, Porsche is just like that: you can’t pinpoint the exact name, but you know the experience was great. Luckily, they do know that when it comes to models and concepts, the name should be easy to understand and remember. Meet the Mission S , with the ‘S’ standing either for that long German word or, easier to remember, for ‘supercar.’
This is basically their manifesto concept car for “the brand's evolved design identity” and what’s coming soon above the 911 series – a new flagship sports car with a mid-engine platform and not fully electrified. Unfortunately, the speculation about the flat-eight engine has not been confirmed just yet because the company hasn’t revealed any technical specifications; thus we don’t know any performance figures, pricing, or a production timeline for the new sports car.
Instead, they talked about all other things. First, the location: the new prototype was presented on a pier in Queens, New York, with a view of the Manhattan skyline beyond. This is where the first picture of a mid-engined Porsche 550 Spyder was taken back in 1953. The Porsche Mission S “provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years,” explains Michael Leiters, Chairman of the Executive Board of Porsche AG .
“At the same time, the Mission S represents a mid-engined super sports car platform positioned above the 911 – not as a one-off hypercar, but as a permanent and versatile addition to our customer offering,” adds Leiters. So, at least we know that a series-production model is coming after this concept, just like it happened with the Porsche Mission E from 2015 and its subsequent alter-ego in production, the Porsche Taycan, which landed in 2019.
Hopefully, this time around we’re not going to wait four more years to see the production version, as the Porsche Mission S looks production-ready with just a few modifications. The design is typical for Porsche but in order to set it apart from the 911, we can easily see a long-tail style, with Porsche claiming influences from the 917 (the fan-like cooling element above the enginee), GT1, and especially the 959 for the exterior.
Inside, Porsche is adapting to the ‘screenless’ current that has emerged after automakers bathed their cars in pillar-to-pillar displays that crashed and left people stranded with no access to simple functions like AC controls.
So, the Mission S takes cues from the 550 Spyder and 356 instead, and physical controls and switches are a big part of the experience, although they also combine analog and digital elements like the reworked Sport Chrono clock or the five round analog gauges that have digital displays behind them, creating an interesting 3D-like effect. There’s no center display – just a retractable smartphone holder with MagSafe technology.

Tesla has finally re-unveiled its next-generation Roadster , originally unveiled in quite different form back in 2017. So since I did a technical breakdown of how it would work last time, I thought I’d give a quick update with what we know about the new version.
Back in 2017, the Roadster was unveiled as the car that would “give a hard-core smack down to gasoline powered cars.”
At the time, electric cars had already proven themselves with extremely quick acceleration numbers. But there weren’t many true electric sportscars (except, of course, the original Tesla Roadster from 2008, the car that started it all).
The next-gen Roadster was intended to change that, with a smaller, low-to-the-ground car built for speed, rather than comfort or efficiency. Of course, you’d still get some of those other goals as with any EV, but the idea was to win races, to beat gas cars around a track.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
And then…. a decade happened. It’s been almost 9 years since that car was first shown off, and Tesla has not released it. Meanwhile, plenty of other companies have released their own electric sportscars, and set records in doing so.
The Rimac Nevera R hit 300km/h (186mph) a full 3.5 seconds faster than a Bugatti Chiron Super Sport, the Xiaomi SU7 Ultra – made by a smartphone company – set a Nürburgring record , and Porsche went even faster, electrically . And another Chinese company, BYD, showed off that its car can jump , an artifact of its active suspension system.
There are even some tricky, fully track-focused EVs that have beaten every car ever with truly videogame-like performance, and the ability to drive upside down – you can even buy it .
So the path Tesla intended to forge is looking less like an untamed wild, and more like a well-tread trail at this point. Maybe everyone hasn’t marched on it, but Tesla is no longer the first.
But Tesla has had the most impressive demo , you have to give it that.
In its demo, it made some wild claims about the car – and then backed them up. Musk said the car would be able to fly, and it did. It did a flip in the air as well. It accelerated from 0-60 in under 1 second, a number that no other car has gotten even close to. It drove upside down.
How did it do all these things, and what do they mean? Will they help the car beat every track record around the world, as Musk promised tonight? Well, it’s time for a quick primer on vehicle dynamics.
(For the purposes of this article, we’re going to treat everything that happened tonight as if it was real, not faked. While a lot of it looked surprising, we do know that fan cars are real, rocket boosters could increase acceleration, and we’ve seen flying machines that self-right with small gas thrusters, so it’s all plausible enough, even if the car’s movements in the air looked much quicker than you’d expect out of a car. Besides, it’s lazy to just say “it’s all fake” – we’d rather try to examine what seems plausible, and what doesn’t, and just use this as a jumping off point to teach people a bit about vehicle dynamics. So strap in.)
Driving upside-down
The first demo showed the Roadster driving up a hot wheels-like track, going fully vertical, and then upside down.
This was accomplished through a “fan car” system, like the McMurtry Spierling, the other car which drove upside down and was mentioned above. Tesla calls it a “multi-mode suction system.”
Fans on the vehicle are used to create a low pressure zone underneath the car, causing ambient air pressure to push the car against the surface it’s stuck to. This is enabled by skirts underneath the vehicle which seal off the vehicle underside so air can’t ingress into the low pressure zone.
This was described in a patent , and is a clever improvement on McMurtry’s system and previous fan car systems, as it allows the skirts to be adjusted so the car can be used in a wider array of circumstances other than smooth track surfaces.
The downforce numbers on Tesla’s display are incredibly high, and seem potentially unreal to me. There’s no need for 4,700kg of downforce on what is presumably a sub-2,000kg car. Musk did mention that Tesla wanted to keep the car “light”, and while many supercars these days push 2,000kg and more, there’s no way a 2 seater is that much heavier than that benchmark…right?
In comparison to the McMurtry Spierling, that car is around 1,000kg and pulls around 2,000kg of downforce to do the things it does. So Tesla is not just running more ridiculous downforce numbers, but also running a larger ratio of weight to downforce than McMurtry’s car. It’s not completely out of the question that it’s running 4,700kg, but that number is still surprisingly large to me and I wouldn’t be surprised if some liberties were taken.
A hint can be seen in other statements about the Roadster’s capabilities – Tesla says it will be capable cornering at 2G, which is plenty impressive enough, though the Spierling claims it can pull up to 3 lateral Gs in a corner.
Jumping off the ramp, then landing. Also, a kickflip
The next trick involved driving up the ramp, jumping off the end and then landing.
This uses the vehicle’s “cold gas thrusters” that have been placed around the car.
Tesla announced separately that the car would come with three trim levels: Performance, Thrust, and Rocket. Rocket is the only one that is “air ready,” and has cold gas thrusters mounted around the vehicle, including underneath, which allow it to fly for short distances.
This is done by compressing air and holding it in tanks onboard the vehicle. While other trim levels are 2-seaters, the “Rocket” trim only has one seat – with the space for the other seat presumably taken up by larger gas tanks so the car has enough juice to fly for short distances.
Admittedly, I know less about rockets than I do about car dynamics, so I have little useful to say about how realistic it is to hold enough gas to produce enough force to do these stunts with a full-size vehicle. But I can tell you what benefits they would provide if they do work as Tesla says they will.
Tesla also showed off the car doing a “kickflip” over the rest of its vehicles, which uses the same technology as the jump did.
This made for an impressive demo, but offers no real performance benefit in terms of driving.
The fan car system provides additional downforce – this is because tires can only work so hard, and adding apparent weight to a car while maintaining its mass (yes, these are two different things) can make those tires work harder. This helps in basically anything you would want to use tires for – so, y’know, every aspect of vehicle performance.
But rockets that push the car upwards do not do any such thing. Those provide “upforce,” which is a word that nobody has uttered because it’s not something you want – unless you’re trying to play a trick on Mark Webber . Pushing the car upwards just makes the tires work less, and hurts performance by a lot.
Worse, including the thrusters for this system adds weight and complexity. That means another thing that can break, and another thing that slows the vehicle down. As Musk said, Acceleration = Force / Mass, so if you add mass, you are decreasing acceleration.
So the jumping is just a party trick, and will not help with performance.
However , the side thrusters could add cornering capability. Downforce makes tires work harder, which is good, but another thing you can do is just not make the tires work at all. By shooting air out of the side of the car during a corner, you are adding lateral acceleration through something other than the tires, so even when the tires are maxed out in the amount of lateral acceleration they can provide, your jets are providing a little more.
(The car will also have steer-by-wire, which should help make cornering easier for a driver, allowing tight turns with less steering input at lower speeds)
So the jump is dumb, but the side thrusters could do something. Which leads us to the more important thrusters: on the rear.
0-60 in 1 second, aided by thrusters
Then Tesla showed a recorded 0-60 test utilizing rear thrusters, wherein the vehicle reached 60mph in 1 second.
Tesla recorded a 0-60 time in 1.0 seconds. That’s almost a record. It says it can go faster.
Later in the show, Tesla did a live demonstration, and claimed that the car hit 60mph in 0.81 seconds, after some technical difficulties with the timer. Tesla later said, in a tweet, that the top-spec version of the car would be able to hit 0-60 in under 0.59 seconds.
Cold gas thrusters strike again here, with four ports at the rear of the vehicle that push a huge plume of gas behind it. These produce 80 kilo-Newtons of force, a number that is used to measure rocket force but does not translate well to horsepower.
Much as described above, if you are at the limit of what tires can do, you can try to find force some other way. The thrusters push the car forward even when the tires can’t push any harder, which enables the car to essentially break the same physics laws that every other car is limited by.
The “fan car” system does help with forward acceleration too, the same way it helps with all other types of lateral acceleration. But the rockets out the back are what give it that extra oomph, allowing it to hit 60mph in under a second, and seemingly in only a few car lengths worth of distance.
Importantly , we don’t know the specifics of this test, which do matter for 0-60 times. Often, 0-60 tests include a “one foot rollout,” where the timer doesn’t start counting until the car starts moving at least a foot. That first foot can take a while for some cars (typically, electric cars accomplish the rollout portion faster, due to high low-end torque), but it’s just how the tests have been done for a while.
That might matter more than usual here, because Tesla clearly activated the thrusters well in advance of when the car started moving, as can be seen in slow-motion video shown during the event here .
With frame-by-frame analysis, the car is still not moving, even after the gas thrusters have started spinning up.
If the thrusters take some time to “wind up,” then they’re less useful for certain types of acceleration tasks – and give back some of the benefits of electric propulsion, the instant torque. Hopefully Tesla has not just invented the electric version of turbo lag.
Moveable wing
The car has an adjustable rear wing , which is perhaps the most “traditional” performance improvement on the car.
This is one of multiple wing configurations
These exist in many vehicles these days, and solve the primary problem of wings.
When people talk about “coefficient of drag” or Cd, which has become a popular stat to quote on an EV, everyone accepts that a lower number is better. If your car makes less drag, it’s more efficient, which means it can go farther with the energy it has. (cross-sectional area also counts – a large car with a low Cd can still lose more energy to drag than a small car with a lower Cd, because a larger car simply pushes more air around).
But drag sometimes offers a performance benefit. Formula One cars actually have extremely high drag coefficients – the most efficient EVs get close to 0.2 Cd, but an F1 car can have a drag coefficient of 0.7 or even 1.0 or higher.
This is because F1 cars actually use all that air for downforce. Instead of letting the air flow smoothly around the vehicle, they actively try to push the air upwards, which in turn pushes the car downwards (Newton’s third law of motion, equal and opposite reactions), which allows the tires to work better.
The problem is that when the car is going in a straight line, it doesn’t need that much downforce. At top speed, that downforce is just drag, which slows the car down.
So, active aerodynamics solves this problem. If you can put up a wing to push air down when you want it, then hide the wing so it lets the air fly by at higher speeds, you can have the best of both worlds. More downforce when cornering, and less drag at high speed.
The concept overall is called “aerodynamic efficiency.” How much downforce you can get through a certain method without adding more drag. A wing offers good downforce, but lots of drag – an active wing helps eliminate the drag downside. (and going back to the fan car system above, that offers a lot of downforce with little drag)
Battery size?
At the original Roadster unveiling in 2017, Tesla said the car would have a 600 mile range. This made headlines, and people thought it was a big deal, or thought it was impossible that the car would have so much more range than everything else on the market.
But range numbers don’t really matter. It’s entirely possible to make an EV with a thousand mile range, but the problem is that car would be terrible. You’d have to spend too much space on batteries, they’d be too heavy, they’d be expensive, and you’d get diminishing returns because the more battery you add, the more battery you have to add to move the weight of that battery around, etc.
So 600 miles of range was kind of bad news for the Roadster. The main reason it had so much range is because EV batteries have a careful balance of many considerations – energy density, power density, cycle life, temperature response, charging speed, and so on and so forth.
At the time, Tesla’s chosen chemistry was rather high on energy density, but comparatively lower on power density. Energy is how much range you have in the battery, and power is how quickly you can get that energy out of it.
So, similar to needing to add more batteries to get more energy onboard the car, Tesla also had to add more batteries to get more power out of the car. If Tesla wanted to get the Roadster up to 1,000hp+, it would need a massive battery – and that was the point behind the “600 mile range.”
Now, we’re hearing that the new version of the next-gen Roadster will have a smaller battery, with Tesla only saying it will have a range of “over 300 miles.”
We don’t know if this is because the car will have less power than originally planned, or if Tesla has managed to get more power out of its cells… but it’s probably a bit of both.
Here you can see the four rear thrusters
It’s likely relying on its boosters and fan car system to pick up the performance slack and reach the absurd numbers Tesla is promising, and realizes that a gigantic battery is not as necessary once you have other ways to push the wheels around.
The location of the battery is of interest too – in Tesla’s photos, the seating position looks quite high, which suggests that the battery is low in the vehicle, as is the case on most of Tesla’s other vehicles.
This driver is sitting high enough that there looks to be a battery between him and the bottom of the car.
This offers a lower center of gravity, which helps with cornering. But it also means a higher seating position, which feels less “sporty.” The original 2008 Roadster actually had the battery placed behind the cockpit, leading vehicle balance to feel like a mid-engined car. The upcoming Porsche 718 EV has a similar configuration.
A low-slung battery will make the Roadster’s cornering feel more neutral, but perhaps less “fun” than a tail-heavy vehicle. Between that and the fan car system, it will probably feel like it’s on rails.
Edit: On further examination, a couple frames of the “kickflip” portion of the video show the underbody of the car
This does not look like Tesla’s typical underbody, which is usually flat, as the battery is there. An underbody with lots of parts hanging off of it is bad for aerodynamics, so this is one of the benefits of putting a battery on the bottom of an EV.
This frame also leads us to the possibility that this car may not have had a battery in it at all. Which could help to explain the car’s fast movements in the air, if it was a thousand pounds lighter than a production vehicle might be… and also another reason that nobody was allowed near the kick-flipping cars to examine them closely. So I know I said at the start that I would take this whole thing seriously, but keep your conspiracy hats handy, boys and girls.
Top speed: rockets probably don’t do much
Tesla quotes top speed at over 230mph. It says that number will only be reachable by the Rocket version of the car, but we’re skeptical that the rockets will have much effect at top speed.
At high speed, your tires are not working very hard to accelerate the car (they’re still working hard, and you need special rated tires for high speed operation, but they are no longer the thing limiting acceleration). Most of your power is going to defeating air drag (which goes up exponentially with speed), and the relative force between the tires and the road is quite minimal.
So the whole point of the rockets (and the fan car system) is nullified here – you don’t need to find another method to take stress off the tires, because the wind is what’s stopping you, not the tires.
Using the rear thrusters for a boost when you reach top speed could help add a few more mph, but as we don’t know how much capacity the tanks have, any top speed benefit may not last for long. The rockets are better used in corners, anyway, I’d say.
We don’t know the tanks’ capacity, but we do know Tesla used different cars for each demo, which could be due to a capacity limitation
So when Tesla claims the Rocket trim can go 230mph, but doesn’t quote a top speed for other trims, this could be due to some other factor. (During the presentation, Musk also mused if the car should be able to reach at least mach 0.5 – which would be ~380mph at sea level, which is unlikely, given the current record is 308.34mph, with an asterisk )
Perhaps the Rocket trim is lighter because of the removal of the second seat (though it loses some of that weight reduction through the addition of tanks + useless downward-pointing thrusters), perhaps it comes with higher-rated tires or a more lenient software governor, or maybe it uses a different or larger battery than the other models. We just don’t know yet, but we hope to get more information soon.
How practical are these thrusters?
Another company, Dreame, a Chinese robot vacuum maker, also proposed using thrusters on an electric hypercar – but it was going to use solid rocket boosters rather than cold gas thrusters. Those would be one-time-use, and need to be recharged each time. It would have made 100kN of thrust and hit 0-60 in 0.9 seconds, but Dreame cancelled the project , which seemed inevitable.
A cold gas thruster is a much better idea, since it doesn’t need to be recharged with solid rocket fuel each time.
But it does need to fill its tanks with pressurized gas, and we don’t know how long that will take, or how much energy it will take. Will the car be able to fill the tanks on straightaways, then deplete them on turns? If so, how long of a straightaway does it need? And will that divert power from the wheels to the air compressors at high speeds, when you’re already taxing the battery to the max at high speeds?
Or, is the party trick only a once-every-few-minutes sort of thing, and you won’t be able to use it for more than a few turns before heading back to the pits?
Tesla seems to think it will be enough to set track records, but that seems to be already possible with the fan car system. McMurtry is setting track records with its Spierling, and it doesn’t have any thrusters out the back or sides.
The radius of debris and smoke runs in the tens of meters
Finally, will you even be able to use them at all on anything other than a closed course? In today’s demo, the crowd was hundreds of yards away, which is a fair precaution for the first demonstration of a car doing a kickflip.
But it wasn’t just the kickflip that was concerning. The plume of gas sprayed out of the back of the car on acceleration, or on turning, seemed massive. It went tens of meters away.
So it certainly doesn’t seem like it should usable on public roads, as debris from the road would be kicked up into other cars, pedestrians, or whatever. Tesla says the “Rocket” is invite-only, and is “not approved for public road use.” But it says nothing under the “Thrust” trim entry, despite that it has the rear thrusters, which could cause plenty of damage.
Even on a closed track, you don’t want to be blowing tire marbles (discarded bits of rubber from tires) into a crowd beside the track, or knocking over marshals or braking boards or blowing all the hair off of too-adventurous squirrels that get too close to the track. It just seems impractical.
Heck, can a human even use these systems at all? For the demos, nobody was in the car. The movements in the air seemed incredibly rapid, much more rapid than you’d expect any several-thousand-pound object would be able to move in the air.
The speed of the acceleration displayed in the air would be at minimum disorienting to any average person. This is the sort of thing that fighter pilots train for years to do. And we’re just going to let people buy the car with Rocket mode and operate it, even as an “invite-only” product? Where? How? What happens if they have a medical episode? Will cars come with a G-suit to stop you from blacking out while operating flight mode? What happens to that compressed air in a crash?

Networking
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-2
At OCP 2026, we saw something that looked absolutely awesome. Walking by the HPE booth, we saw an AMD Helios tray set up and open on the show floor. It stopped me in my tracks, so I thought folks would like to see it.
This is the AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 Switch Tray at OCP 2026
Oftentimes, when we open up huge switches, we see a lot of internal PCB. This is totally different since it is a double-wide tray with side-by-side switches and lots of copper.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-1
You can see the HPE QFX5252 label on the front latch, which is huge. Because there is so much connectivity on the back, and the back panel is long and needs to blind mate, the insertion force required for a switch tray like this into the Helios rack is significant. As a result, these levers are very long.
Since this is two big switch chips in a 1OU tray, it needs to be liquid cooled. You can see the internal liquid cooling manifolds distributing liquid to the various blocks.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-3
There are two switch chips inside, which are Broadcom Tomahawk 6 102.6T switches. At first, you might wonder why these are not Broadcom Tomahawk Ultra chips , since that might make sense for a scale-up architecture. The current generation Tomahawk Ultra is a 112G PAM4 SerDes switch (so 512 lanes of PAM4-112G.) That is not enough for Helios which is using 224G PAM4 SerDes. As a result, these need to be Tomahawk 6.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-2
Now, the next part is very different. AMD and HPE-Juniper are not just slinging Tomahawk 6 on some PCBs and calling it a day. You will notice that the cabled connections to the rear high-density fabric connectors for the Helios rack cable cartridges are quite far from the Tomahawk 6 switch chips. Some of them in particular are very far from the switch chips. The liquid cooling blocks between those cable connectors and the switch chip are apparently retimers. AMD is big on retimers while NVIDIA has worked to remove them.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-6
Aside from the switches and retimers, let us talk about the cables.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-7
When we say copper inside a rack, and why we will eventually go to co-packaged optics, this is a great illustration. In the QFX5252, retimers extend reach so we can reliably scale up within the rack. Then we need an enormous array of copper cables. CPO would simplify this design. I will probably use these photos when explaining the “why” for CPO in the future.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-4
You can see the fans and airflow guides over heatsinks for some other components. Unlike NVIDIA’s push to move fans out of the AI rack, AMD Helios still uses fans and air cooling for some other bits in the tray.
AMD Helios HPE Juniper QFX5252 OCP 2026-5
Overall, very cool.
Final Words
We previously covered the QFX5252 at HPE Discover 2026, but seeing the switch tray assembled and on the show floor was really cool. A lot is going on here, and it is very different from the normal rackmount switches we see. One of the biggest differences, of course, is that it is designed to scale up within a rack instead of out of front-panel connectors.
HPE Discover 2026 HPE Juniper Networking QFS5252
Of course, if you are into networking, check out our Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab tour that we were finally able to publish yesterday.
As a fun aside, I was at HPE’s booth looking at this switch tray when Pradeep Sindhu walked over and started looking at the switch with the HPE-Juniper team and me. For me, it was neat because the last time I saw Pradeep was when we did this Fungible DPU-based Storage Cluster Hands-on Look back in the pandemic era in 2020. It was neat having Juniper’s co-founder and former CTO look at the big switch tray while I was there.

Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama.
The project expands the plant’s manufacturing footprint to more than 735,000 square feet. The expansion adds 100,000 square feet of new space and converts 85,000 square feet of office space into factory floor space for automated, high-precision machining.
Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025. Lockheed said it has added more than 30 high-precision machines in recent months and expects to install nearly 100 additional machines by the end of 2026.
Lockheed also said Hadrian, a California-based manufacturing startup, will install 24 automated machines at the Grand Prairie facility to produce missile parts. Lockheed employees will operate the equipment, which is expected to be up and running by early 2027. The project follows a memorandum of understanding the two companies signed in December 2025.
“The warfighter can’t wait on peacetime timelines,” Hadrian CEO Chris Power said in the release. “Rebuilding the Arsenal of Freedom at the scale America needs will take partnerships that combine expertise and speed, and this is what that looks like.”
The buildout supports a series of framework agreements the Defense Department has signed with Lockheed since January, designed to boost missile production and lead to long-term contracts. The first aims to increase PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to roughly 2,000 interceptors per year over seven years.
The Army followed with a $4.7 billion contract in April, then converted it in July into a seven-year production contract worth about $58.6 billion in total.
A separate THAAD framework , signed in January, led to a June contract from the Missile Defense Agency worth more than $35 billion to quadruple interceptor production. Lockheed and the Pentagon announced similar agreements for the Precision Strike Missile on March 25 and for the AIM-260 on Sept. 17.
“Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both,” said Jim Taiclet, Lockheed’s chairman, president and CEO. “By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale.”
“This expansion is more than just a new facility; it is a stronger supply chain and a more resilient industrial base,” said Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment.

Tesla Finally Unveils the Roadster: It Does the Kick Flip Mid-Air, Goes From 0 to 60 in 0.81 Seconds
41 photos
Photo: Tesla
The second-generation Tesla Roadster has officially been revealed as a ground-up redesign with aerospace technology, developed in collaboration with SpaceX, where else but at the SpaceX testing facility in Texas? Yes, the Roadster can "fly," it does the kick-flip mid-air and it goes from 0 to 60 mph in well under a second. Footage from the event looks like a sci-fi movie scene.
Tesla first unveiled the concept car that previewed the production Roadster back in 2017, alongside the Semi, planning to officially unveil the production model in 2018 and send it into production by 2019. Fast forward to 2026, and we finally get to the end of Elon Musk's long series of overpromising and underdelivering.
Tesla has been p ostponing the unveiling of the Roadster time and again, blaming development issues, April Fool's Day, and even the weather. Luckily, it did not rain in Texas last night, and here it is, in all its glory, putting an end to nearly a decade of speculation and looking miles apart from the concept that previewed it nearly a decade ago.
The electric supercar comes with retro-inspired looks, which have been blended into a modern appearance, reminding of the aggressively wedge-shaped Lamborghinis of the 1970s and 1990s. The front fascia drops steeply down into an ultra-low point with sharp geometric creases, reminiscent of the nose design of the Diablo .
Photo: Tesla The all-new Roadster also gets the oh-look-at-me scissor doors for Tesla-typical drama, a layout that debuted with the Lamborghini Countach back in 1974. The Roadster retains the low-slung stance, but ditches the flowing silhouette for a much angular design. An active deployable rear spoiler that works in tandem with the vehicle's computer systems is designed to stabilize the car during acceleration or heavy braking.
The cabin of the all-new Tesla Roadster features a minimalist, driver-focused layout with a two-seat configuration. Tesla's yoke steering wheel is paired with a steer-by-wire system like you get in the Cybertruck, and new metal paddles on the steering column. Expectedly, the touchscreen with distinctive Mars-red interface theme, controls most of the functions of the car.
And the drama is far from over. As Elon Musk has been promising, the car does feature short-duration "flying" capabilities with the help of compressed air thrusters. Well, he also promised that the Cybertruck would float , and it would go to the bottom of the ocean and stay there forever, just like Musk's first-generation Roadster went to space with little to no chance at all of ever setting wheels on planet Earth.
This time, the demonstration that took place at the SpaceX facility in Texas last night proves the flying is real when the supercar is equipped with the Rocket package. The package includes ten cold-gas thruster nozzles, integrated into the body panels. The rear license plate area is designed to mechanically move out of the way when the main rear thrust tanks fire.
Photo: Tesla High-pressure compressed air, primarily nitrogen, is stored in a massive composite-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) tank, which is located right behind the cabin. The vehicle counts on ultra-fast electric actuators to handle the gas jets mid-air, allowing the onboard computer to stabilize the car and dictate orientation while in "flight." The compressed cold-gas thrusters generate over 80kN of raw thrust.
No, you won't wave looking upwards to the Tesla driver traveling above the highway. Rather than long-distance travel, the Tesla Roadster is capable of short aerial stunts, and the driver won't need any special pilot license. However, the extreme rocket-thruster configuration may face strict street-legality hurdles in various markets. Furthermore, this single-seat flight-capable Rocket variant is invite-only, meaning you cannot publicly reserve it.
During the demo in Texas, an uncrewed prototype rolled toward a line-up of other Teslas, fired the thrusters, shot into the air, executed a complete 360-degree roll that Tesla dubbed the "kick flip," and used its air jets to cushion its landing back on the ground.
Furthermore, using an underbody vacuum-suction "fan sucker" system, the Roadster drove up a vertical ramp, came to a dead stop completely upside down, and clung to the surface using pure ground-effect suction in what seems like a sci-fi movie scene.
Photo: Tesla The "flying" Tesla also shows off on the ground, with a time from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in a mind-blowing 0.81 seconds, which makes it the fastest-accelerating car in the world. However, still no word on specs, as Tesla keeps horsepower and torque figures behind closed doors.
If the rumors are anything to go by, then the Roadster’s rear-mounted dual-motor setup will generate a megawatt of power, which translates to a neck-snapping 1,500 horsepower. Tesla is testing our mathematics skills, revealing that this new setup should deliver one-third more power than the Model S Plaid, which had 1,020 horsepower.
Just as a reminder, the first-generation Tesla Roadster debuted in 2008 with a three-phase four-pole AC induction electric motor which generated 248 horsepower (252 metric horsepower). The auto world has changed a bit in the meantime.
While the first-generation Roadster was offered in both right- and left-hand drive, Tesla has confirmed that the production vehicle will be manufactured strictly as a left-hand drive vehicle, leaving its launch in right-hand drive markets like the UK or Australia unconfirmed.
The all-new Tesla Roadster will go into production at the Giga Texas plant in 2028. At least that is what Tesla says. They'd better keep that promise this time. The final price is still unconfirmed. Besides, why confirm it in 2026 when we all know it can go through the roof by 2028?

Until the Tesla Roadster, “there was only one car in the flying car market,” Alef said. To welcome Tesla to the race, Alef released a video of its flying car flying over the new Roadster.
Alef flies over Tesla Roadster as flying car race heats up
Does it drive like a car, or fly like a plane? Alef’s flying car can do both. After a video of its electric flying car went viral last year as it jumped over a Tesla Cybertruck , Alef Aeronautics is at it again.
Alef released a new video of its flying car on Thursday flying over a Tesla Roadster to “welcome it to the flying car race.”
The California-based startup threw a slight jab, saying that the “Tesla Roadster today became the second flying car in history, following Alef.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Alef just completed its 1,000th logged flight, which happened to be a Tesla Roadster. The Tesla Roadster and Alef’s flying car share several things. Both use electric powertrains, are all-wheel drive, and share the same early investor: Tim Draper.
How do they differ? Alef uses distributed electric propulsion (DEP), while Tesla’s Roadster is expected to use thrusters.
Alef’s flying car flies over Tesla Roadster (Source: Alef Aeronautics)
Alef’s flying car has a wing-forming body, a rotating cabin, and uses air rather than stored compressed gas for liftoff. According to Alef, its vehicle is lighter, allowing for a “full-vehicle ballistic parachute.”
A flying car is not the same as an eVTOL (electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing) vehicle. The main difference is that it can drive, park, and be used like any other car.
Alef developed its first flying-car prototype in 2019. In 2022, it revealed its first full-size prototype, the Model A, with a 220-mile driving range and a 110-mile flight range.
Alef flies flying car over Tesla Cybertruck, Roadster, and other vehicles (Source: Alef Aeronautics)
By 2023, Alef’s flying car received an FAA Special Airworthiness Certification , making it the first real flying car recognized by the US government. The Tesla Roadster still has to go through the FAA Type Certification, which can take several years.
Last year, Alef released the first public video of its Model Zero Ultralight driving and flying, including over a Tesla Cybertruck.
CEO Jim Dukhovny introduces the Model A electric flying car at the Detroit Auto Show (Source: Alef)
“Welcome, Tesla, to the flying car race; we’ve been here alone for eleven years,” Jim Dukhovny, Alef’s CEO, said.
Having competition is “a good thing,” he said. “It proves the market, establishes a separate flying car category, creates industry for lobbying specific regulations, brings investor focus, helps compare technology, and creates a benchmark to measure against.”
Alef has received over 3,600 pre-orders worth $1 billion. In December, the company began hand-building the first flying cars to deliver to customers from its facility in Silicon Valley, California.
Alef’s flying car flies over Tesla Roadster, Cybertruck, and other vehicles (Source: Alef Aeronautics)
The first batch is expected to be delivered to a limited number of early buyers by the end of 2026. According to Alef, they will be for “the purpose of testing flying cars in the real-world environment, under very controlled conditions.”
As production ramps up in 2027, the company plans to train and help early adopters use the flying car.
While owning a flying car sounds fun. It likely won’t be cheap at first. Alef’s first flying car is expected to start at $299,999. You can pre-order one on its website with a $150 deposit, or you can secure a spot in the priority queue for $1,500.

Waze Does More Harm Than Good, Study Reveals: Drivers Use It To Avoid Speeding Tickets
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
I really don’t think we needed a study to figure this out, but new research conducted by an Australian university highlights the ugly truth. People use Waze to avoid speeding tickets and escape unpunished when they go over the limit.
The University of the Sunshine Coast Research published a new paper to explain that navigation apps that include a crowdsourcing component eventually do more harm than good. The reason is simple: they help speeding drivers dodge tickets.
University of the Sunshine Coast Research Associate Dr. Levi Anderson said applications like Waze only “provide a short-term, localised benefit in reducing speeds and crash risks at particular sites for limited times.”
This is because an alert appearing on Waze makes people slow down , but most drivers end up speeding again after they go past the location where the alert was pinned. More specifically, when a driver running Waze receives an alert that a speed trap was reported ahead, he slows down until he goes past the speed trap and then accelerates, going over the limit again and, therefore, dodging a potential speeding ticket.
The University representative also said that Waze is a “long-term detriment to road safety,” as drivers rely on the data it offers to speed.
Photo: Dendermonde police department So what exactly did the researchers discover during the study?
First, the researchers used a laser device specifically to measure the speed of incoming vehicles before and after getting a Waze alert. The test was conducted in multiple locations, including on the highway, as the purpose was to figure out where drivers tend to rely on Waze data the most.
The laser speed measurement device was used to clock the speed of over 9,000 vehicles in industrial areas, school zones, residential streets, and highways.
The results speak for themselves.
Photo: Dendermonde police department When driving on a road with a 100 kph speed limit (that’s around 62 mph for our American friends), the number of vehicles going over the limit drops from 64% to no more, no less than 12% after getting an alert on Waze.
This means that out of all cars driving on the road when the test was conducted, 64% were going faster than the limit. When Waze issued a notification, the percentage fell dramatically, as drivers tried to avoid the speeding ticket.
Unfortunately, the same thing happens in those places where speeding is even more dangerous.
Case in point, school zones. In this case, while drivers are speeding, they don’t seem to react to Waze alerts as fast and as responsively as they do when they see a police alert. The drop in the number of people speeding in a school zone is concerning - from 64.3% to 38.5%.
Waze’s crowdsourcing component relies on a gigantic user base. Drivers on the road run the app to send reports about what happens on the road. Waze supports a wide variety of traffic reports, including multiple types of speed traps, broken traffic lights, accidents, blocked lanes, roadworks, flooded roads, and objects on the road.
When a user sends a traffic report, Waze receives the data and generates an alert for the rest of the users whose routes include the flagged location. In the case of speed traps, a user can pin the police car on the map, with everybody else then getting a notification on the screen. Waze also prompts users to confirm the existence of a traffic report.
The study reveals that a speed trap appears on Waze after only 14 minutes. This means that once a police car stops on the side of the road to install a speed radar, Waze needs just 14 minutes (that’s on average, because the time could be significantly lower depending on the Waze user base at the time of speed enforcement) to start showing alerts to other drivers in the region.
Photo: Dendermonde police department The only solution, the study shows, is to rely on “shorter, geographically dispersed deployments” for speed traps. In plain English, this means that police should set up speed traps in a specific region and move to another in the 14-minute window. Obviously, this is highly inconvenient for police officers in the first place, but this is the only way to avoid the Waze reports.
So why did some people not slow down during the test? The reasons are unclear, but the researchers believe that either they weren’t using Waze in their cars or they were going only a few miles per hour over the speed limit, therefore dodging a speeding ticket and only getting a warning.
Waze is not the only application that supports crowdsourced traffic reports, with Google Maps also offering similar functionality and even importing police reports from Waze. Waze is available on most platforms, including Android, iPhone, Android Auto, and CarPlay. Like Google Maps (Waze is also owned by Google), Waze is free for everybody, no matter where you install it.
